lead: A power divider takes one input and delivers set fractions of it to two or more outputs; run backwards it is a combiner. An attenuator lowers the power by a known number of decibels while staying matched at both ends. Together they set signal levels in antenna feeds, phased arrays, receiver front ends and test benches. The questions to ask of each are the same: are the ports matched, are the outputs isolated, and where does any lost power go?
prereq: You need: dB and dBm, and the S-matrix tests in S-parameters and the scattering matrix, including the proof in Waveguide tees that a lossless reciprocal three-port cannot be matched.

blocks.text: A lossless T-junction joins an input line of impedance Z₀ to two output lines Z₁ and Z₂. For the input to be matched, the two outputs in parallel must equal Z₀: 1/Z₁ + 1/Z₂ = 1/Z₀. The input voltage is shared, so each output takes power in proportion to 1/Z.

blocks.where: P₁ is the input power and P₂, P₃ the output powers. For a 2 : 1 split from 50 Ω: Z₁ = 75 Ω takes ⅔ and Z₂ = 150 Ω takes ⅓; 75 ∥ 150 = 50 Ω.

blocks.text: The input is matched, but the outputs are not: looking back into the 75 Ω arm one sees 50 ∥ 150 = 37.5 Ω, a reflection of (37.5 − 75)/(37.5 + 75) = −0.333. The outputs are also not isolated. That is the three-port theorem at work.

A resistive divider puts a resistor of Z₀/3 (16.7 Ω in a 50 Ω system) in series with each of three ports, joined at a star point. Every port is matched and the network is reciprocal, but half the input power is turned into heat: each output gets P₁/4, which is 6.02 dB below the input. The outputs are not isolated either (S₂₃ = ½, a 6 dB path). It is broadband and cheap, which suits test benches.
The equal-split Wilkinson divider feeds two quarter-wave lines of impedance √2 Z₀ (70.7 Ω for Z₀ = 50 Ω) from the input, and joins their output ends with a resistor R = 2Z₀ (100 Ω).

items: Driven from port 1 with matched outputs, the two output ends are at the same voltage, so no current flows in R. Each λ/4 line transforms the Z₀ load into (√2 Z₀)²/Z₀ = 2Z₀, and two of these in parallel give Z₀: port 1 is matched and the divider is lossless, with half the power at each output (−3.01 dB).

A wave entering output 2 splits: half travels the λ/4 line to port 1, and half crosses R, where it meets the part that went round through the other line. The two parts reaching port 3 are equal and opposite, so port 3 gets nothing: the outputs are isolated, and ports 2 and 3 are matched. The power that does not reach port 1 is absorbed in R.

blocks.where: rows and columns are ports 1 (input), 2 and 3. Matched (zero diagonal), reciprocal (symmetric), isolated (S₂₃ = 0). Column 1 sums to ½ + ½ = 1, but columns 2 and 3 sum to only ½: the matrix is not unitary, and the missing half is the power the resistor absorbs when an output is driven.

blocks.text: So the Wilkinson escapes the three-port theorem by being lossy, but only for waves coming back from the outputs. Match and isolation are exact only at the design frequency, where the lines are a quarter-wave long, and degrade slowly on either side; multi-section versions widen the band. Unequal splits use unequal line impedances and a different resistor.

An attenuator reduces power by A dB and presents Z₀ at both ports. A fixed attenuator (pad) is a T or π network of resistors; a step attenuator switches pads in fixed steps such as 1 dB or 10 dB; a variable attenuator uses a PIN diode whose RF resistance follows its DC bias, or in waveguide a resistive vane moved into the field (the rotary-vane attenuator sets loss by the angle of its vane).

blocks.where: P<sub>in</sub> and P<sub>out</sub> in watts; pads in cascade add: A = A₁ + A₂. A level in dBm falls by A dB through the pad.

blocks.text: T pad: series arms R₁ = Z₀(K − 1)/(K + 1), shunt arm R₂ = 2Z₀K/(K² − 1),   K = 10<sup>A/20</sup>
blocks.where: K is the voltage ratio of the pad. For 10 dB in 50 Ω: K = 3.162, R₁ = 25.97 Ω, R₂ = 35.14 Ω. A π pad of the same loss has series 71.15 Ω and two shunt arms of 96.25 Ω.

blocks.text: The S-matrix of a matched pad is [0 1/K ; 1/K 0]: matched and reciprocal, with column sums 1/K² = 10<sup>−A/10</sup> < 1, so it is lossy by design. The pad must be rated for the power it absorbs, P<sub>in</sub> − P<sub>out</sub>, which for a large pad is nearly all of the input. A pad between a source and a poorly matched load also improves the match the source sees, because a reflection crosses the pad twice and returns 2A dB weaker.

examples.question: A 20 dBm source feeds a matched 6 dB attenuator, followed by an ideal equal Wilkinson divider with matched loads. Find the power at each output in dBm and mW, and the power the attenuator absorbs.
steps: After the pad: 20 − 6 = 14 dBm, that is 100 × 10<sup>−0.6</sup> = 25.12 mW.
The Wilkinson halves the power with no loss when its outputs are matched: 25.12/2 = 12.56 mW at each output.
In dBm: 10 log₁₀ 12.56 = 10.99 dBm, that is 14 − 3.01 dB.
examples.answer: Each output gets 12.56 mW (10.99 dBm, about 11 dBm); the pad absorbs 74.9 mW.
examples.check:
import math
p=100*10**-0.6
print(round(p/2,2), round(10*math.log10(p/2),2), round(100-p,2))

examples.question: Design an equal-split Wilkinson divider for 50 Ω at 2 GHz on a microstrip where the 70.7 Ω line has εeff = 3.0. Then 10 mW is fed into output port 2 with ports 1 and 3 matched: where does it go?
steps: λ₀ = c/f = 3 × 10⁸/2 × 10⁹ = 150 mm; λg = 150/√3.0 = 86.6 mm; each line is λg/4 = 21.65 mm long.
Fed at port 2 (a₂ = √10): column 2 of S has S₁₂ = −j/√2, S₂₂ = 0, S₃₂ = 0.
Port 1 receives |S₁₂|² × 10 = 0.5 × 10 = 5 mW; port 3 receives 0; nothing reflects.
The other 10 − 5 = 5 mW is absorbed in the 100 Ω resistor.
examples.answer: Two 70.7 Ω lines 21.65 mm long and a 100 Ω resistor. Power fed into an output: 5 mW reaches the input, none the other output, and 5 mW heats the resistor. That is how a Wilkinson combiner loses power when its two inputs are unequal.

traps: Taking 3 dB as half the voltage. A 3 dB split halves the power; each output voltage is 1/√2 of the input.
Calling the Wilkinson lossless in every case. It is lossless only from the input with matched outputs; power coming back from an output is half absorbed in the resistor.
Giving a resistive divider a 3 dB loss. Each output of the equal resistive divider is 6.02 dB down, because half the power is dissipated.
Adding dBm to dBm. 20 dBm − 6 dB = 14 dBm; two 20 dBm (100 mW) signals combined make 200 mW = 23 dBm, not 40 dBm.
Rating a pad by its output power. A 20 dB pad fed with 1 W absorbs 0.99 W and must be rated for it.

quiz.q: Define a power divider and an attenuator.
quiz.a: A power divider splits one input into two or more outputs in a set power ratio (and combines when run backwards). An attenuator reduces power by a known number of dB while matched at both ports.

quiz.q: Why can a lossless reciprocal three-port not be matched at all ports? Complete the argument from the off-diagonal conditions.
quiz.a: With a zero diagonal, orthogonality of the columns gives S₁₃S*₂₃ = 0, S₁₂S*₃₂ = 0 and S₂₁S*₃₁ = 0, so at least two of S₁₂, S₁₃, S₂₃ are zero. Then one port has both its couplings zero and a zero reflection, so its column sum is 0, not 1. That contradicts losslessness.

quiz.q: A 10 dBm signal passes through a 3 dB pad and then an ideal equal Wilkinson divider. Find each output in dBm and mW.
quiz.a: 10 − 3 − 3.01 = 3.99 dBm ≈ 4 dBm at each output, that is 10<sup>0.4</sup> = 2.51 mW.

quiz.q: One output of a Wilkinson divider is left open. What happens to the reflected power, and does the other output still get its share?
quiz.a: The open end reflects all the power reaching it. That wave behaves as a wave fed into port 2: half goes back to the input and half is absorbed in the resistor; none reaches port 3. Port 3 still gets the same half of the input power, so the good output is unaffected; the input sees a reflection.

quiz.q: Write the formula for attenuation in dB and the rule for pads in cascade.
quiz.a: A = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub>) dB; cascaded matched pads add, A = A₁ + A₂.

quiz.q: A 0 dBm signal goes through 10 dB and 6 dB pads in cascade. Find the output power.
quiz.a: Total 16 dB, so the output is −16 dBm = 10<sup>−1.6</sup> mW = 0.0251 mW = 25.1 µW.

quiz.q: Find the resistors of a 6 dB T pad for 50 Ω.
A lossless T-junction splits 50 Ω into 75 Ω and 150 Ω lines. Is the 75 Ω output matched?
quiz.a: Looking back from the 75 Ω arm: 50 Ω in parallel with 150 Ω = 37.5 Ω. Γ = (37.5 − 75)/(37.5 + 75) = −0.333, VSWR 2.0. Not matched, as the three-port theorem predicts.

beyond: Wilkinson combiners add the outputs of many transistors in solid-state power amplifiers and feed phased arrays; digital step attenuators set gain under software control. Search for "N-way Wilkinson combiner" and "digital step attenuator".
